## UN condemns attempted Houthi strike on Riyadh as Yemen displacement surges past 130,000

“**We reiterate our condemnation of the continued Houthi cross‑border attacks against Saudi Arabia, including the attempt to target Riyadh**,” UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told journalists at the daily noon briefing, adding that Houthi forces had also struck civilians and energy infrastructure elsewhere in the kingdom.

Mr. Dujarric said the UN remained **“deeply concerned” about the military escalation in and around Yemen**, including Houthi offensives against Saudi-backed Government forces in Ta’iz, Lahj and Marib, and called on all parties to exercise restraint and uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the prohibition on attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The UN’s Special Envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, is in Muscat this week for talks with senior Omani officials and Houthi representatives.
## **Displacement accelerating**
The escalation follows a new wave of clashes between Saudi‑backed Yemeni Government forces and Iran‑backed Houthi militia.
Since early September, Houthi forces have pushed along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and seized territory near the Bab al‑Mandab Strait, a key chokepoint for oil and global shipping.
Saudi Arabia has responded with hundreds of air strikes, and the Houthis have retaliated with drone and missile attacks in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
Nearly 130,000 people have now been forced from their homes across Yemen in the past few weeks, according to the International Organization for Migration ([IOM](https://www.iom.int/)).
## **Thousands fleeing each day**
The numbers are climbing fast: on **18 September, IOM recorded 118,086 displaced people; three days later the figure had risen by 11,352**.

[OCHA](https://www.unocha.org/) told journalists that over the weekend alone, 21,000 households had been displaced across the country since 1 August, most of them in Ta’iz and Lahj, with the figure expected to rise as registration continues.
Ta’iz hosts the most displaced people, with 73,494, followed by Lahj with 33,828, Aden with 8,946 and Al Hodeidah with 8,244, IOM figures show.
**More than 3,100 people have crossed the Red Sea to Djibouti** since the escalation began.

These latest movements add to a decade of conflict, economic collapse and environmental disaster that had already displaced 4.8 million Yemenis, according to the UN refugee agency, [UNHCR](http://www.unhcr.org/).
## **Health system under strain**
Health workers are paying a heavy price. On Friday, **ambulances were attacked** in Lahj governorate, killing a driver and an emergency medical responder.

**Nine health facilities have been damaged**, closed or directly attacked in Ta’iz, Lahj and Al Hodeidah, and hospitals treating the wounded are running short of blood, anaesthesia and surgical supplies, OCHA said.
The UN reproductive health agency ([UNFPA](https://www.unfpa.org/)) estimates that **more than 2,700 pregnant women are among the displaced, with 300 due to give birth within two weeks**.
Key obstetric facilities have closed in Ta’iz, forcing some women to give birth in the open without skilled care.
## **Response hampered**
Insecurity, damaged roads, telecommunications disruptions and damage to Al Makha port are hampering the humanitarian response, UNHCR said.

Humanitarian partners have reached nearly 13,000 displaced households with rapid response kits, and the World Health Organization has delivered surgical supplies and antibiotics to four hospitals in Aden and Marib.

## Areas where FCDO advises against travel
### Saudi Arabia-Yemen border
FCDO advises against:

-   all travel to within 10km of the border with Yemen 
-   all but essential travel to areas between 10km and 80km from the border with Yemen, and extends to include the cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait in Aseer province
Find out more about [why FCDO advises against travel](/foreign-travel-advice/saudi-arabia/regional-risks).
## Regional tensions

Since 13 July, the Houthis (a military group in Yemen) have launched missiles and drones targeting cities, airports, military and energy sites across Saudi Arabia, including Abha, Jizan, Najran, Riyadh, Jeddah and Yanbu, as well as shipping in the Red Sea. Further attacks are possible. Follow Saudi Civil Defence alerts. See [‘Regional risks’ page](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/saudi-arabia/regional-risks).
British nationals currently in the Middle East should be prepared for possible flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruption, and should:

-   read [If you’re affected by a crisis abroad - GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/how-to-deal-with-a-crisis-overseas). This includes guidance on “how to prepare for a crisis” with suggestions on what you might include in your emergency supplies and “what to do in a crisis”
-   follow advice from the local authorities and sign up to FCDO Travel Advice [email alerts](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/saudi-arabia/email-signup)
-   refrain from capturing or sharing images of conflict-related incidents
-   monitor local and international media for the latest information, including updates relating to airports and airspace which could close at short notice. Exercise caution at transport infrastructure, including ports and airports.
-   stay away from areas around oil infrastructure and military facilities
-   keep your departure plans under review, and ensure your travel documents are up to date
-   if you are advised to take shelter, stay indoors or find the nearest safe building or designated shelter. An interior stairwell or a room with as few external walls or windows as possible may provide additional protection. The greatest risk is from falling debris caused by intercepts, and you are safest inside a secure structure

The US and Iran announced a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on 17 June 2026 in relation to the conflict in the Middle East, however the situation in the Middle East remains unpredictable. Before the ceasefire, the Iranian regime had stated its intention to target locations associated with the US and Israel, including organisations, businesses, facilities, and institutions.

## Overview

Houthi attacks against Saudi interests in the Southwestern provinces have resumed in recent weeks. The security situation remains highly volatile.  Civilian infrastructure and energy infrastructure continue to remain a target of Houthi strikes. While these attacks are more common in the Southwestern provinces of Najran, Jazan and Asir, missile and drone threats are not confined to these specific regions and may affect airports, transport hubs, energy infrastructure and other critical facilities, throughout Saudi Arabia.

Military and retaliatory strikes have also continued between the United States and Iran in recent months, with Iranian attacks targeting a number of locations in the Middle East including the Eastern and Riyadh provinces of Saudi Arabia. Whilst this hasn’t occurred in recent weeks, military activity could occur or resume in a sustained way at any time, with US linked locations continuing to remain a target of Iranian strikes.

Travel disruptions and airspace closures could occur at short notice, potentially impacting New Zealanders throughout Saudi Arabia for some time. Our travel advice levels could also change at short notice.
Given this, we strongly encourage New Zealanders to:

-   to register their travel on SafeTravel, as this is the official registration facility for New Zealanders travelling or living overseas. If you’re registered on SafeTravel we are able to: 
-   Contact you if there is a major incident overseas.
-   Send you updates in the event of an emergency. 
-   Send you updates we make to our Travel Advice.
New Zealanders should ensure they follow any shelter orders given by local authorities. These measures are in place to ensure your safety. Before and during the event of a missile or drone strike:

-   **Know how** alerts are communicated in your location (for example, sirens or mobile phone alerts).
    -   Sign up and monitor local and international media to stay informed of developments. If a registration system exists in your area sign up to the alerts issued by local civil defence authorities.  
-   **Know what** to do. Follow the advice of local authorities at all times. This includes any evacuation orders or shelter in place instructions. 
-   **Know where** to go, including whether there are shelters in your location or nearby.
    -   If there are designated shelters, go to one immediately
    -   If there are no designated shelters, immediately move inside a building and ideally to a basement or interior room away from windows. Talk to your residence or hotel, to confirm the best place to shelter in place where you are, should that be necessary.
    -   Shelter in place until you receive an all‑clear notification, or for at least one hour after the last attack or intercept is heard.
-   **Be prepared:** 
    -   Know where likely targets are and avoid these locations, relocating to a safer location if they’re close by. Likely targets include military bases, oil infrastructure, critical infrastructure like airports, power plants and sub-stations, telecommunication sites, de-salination plants and US Linked locations like: US diplomatic facilities (E.g. US Embassies, US Consulates) and identifiably US businesses.
